title: The Best Wines to Serve at a Wedding, According to Industry Pros
summary:
When it comes to wedding wine, somms and beverage directors know best. Here’s their advice, from what to pour and why.

The post The Best Wines to Serve at a Wedding, According to Industry Pros appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Wine has a way of fueling weddings. Its roles may include, but are not limited to: Champagne toasts to the happy couple, glasses that enliven the dance floor, and pours that buffer interactions with quirky relatives and old flames.

While grocery store bottles will certainly be on budget for all of the above, sommeliers (and picky family members) will argue that weddings are special, so it’s not the time to opt for ordinary or everyday wines. 

“It’ssuch a thoughtful touch to avoid the same old Prosecco and grocery store brands people are accustomed to,” says Katy Kindred, founder of Kindred Hospitality restaurant group, which often hosts outdoor and indoor weddings. “Most guests don’t notice when it’s a standard wine, but when your wine is thoughtfully considered, you notice.”

We’re not suggesting you throw out the budget in favor of old vintages and the best of Burgundy. “You want the big day to be special,” Kindred says. “It’s not just a party: it’s the first day of a marriage. But you also want to start off your marriage right by being a good steward of your resources.”

To take the guesswork out of your wedding wine, sommeliers and event experts weigh in on how to pick the perfect big-day bottles.

How to Choose Wine for Weddings

Bryce Faucheaux, general manager of Louisiana’s Old Metairie Bottle Shop, and Missy Auge, wine director at Santa Fe’s Bishop’s Lodge, Auberge Resorts Collection, follow a few rules when selecting bottles for events or weddings.

  • Consider what’s popular. Don’t stick to your own preferences. “Anticipate what people might ask for,” Faucheaux says. “Sauvignon Blanc or a Cabernet Sauvignon–based blend are almost always requested.” Stock accordingly.
  • Order exuberantly. A general rule of thumb is one bottle per person. That may seem like overkill, but it’s better to be left with extras than run dry during dinner.
  • Look locally. “Talk with local wine shops,” Faucheaux says. “They might be able to work with you and negotiate a better price for bulk orders.” Another option? Inquire within nearby wineries—they also may be willing to offer a better price on large orders (added plus: you’re shopping local).
  • Fit the wine to the weather, not just the occasion. “My brother got married in August in New Orleans,” Faucheaux says. “So, I picked some refreshing styles of white wine, as well as a chillable red.” At a winter wedding? You can probably hold off on the pét-nat.
  • Be mindful of the food. “If the wedding is going to focus on seafood, then oaky dark-fruited Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon is probably not the best option,” Faucheaux says. “Loire Valley whites and reds are very easy to work with. Refreshing, mineral-driven styles of Chenin Blanc from Vouvray are always a nice option. As far as reds, Cabernet Franc from Chinon can be very refreshing.”
  • Keep it approachable. “You don’t want to serve really crazy, expensive wine that no one will appreciate or understand, nor do you want to serve wine so obscure that your guests will be afraid of it,” Auge says.
  • And don’t fuss too much: “Choose one white and one red to pass around for dinner, and don’t over-think the pairing too much,” says Auge. “This is a party, not a wine pairing dinner. Just pick something that is easy and tasty to drink on its own.”
  • Split the selection. “Have a few special wines off to the side for the bride and groom,” Faucheaux says. There’s no better time to break open that vintage Champagne or baller Burgundy—the guests will understand. “It is their day, after all, so make sure that they have a couple of their favorite styles,” he adds. “And if you can, save a few bottles for future anniversaries.”
  • Bubbles are for every occasion. “Champagne has gotten very expensive,” says Faucheaux. “So, Prosecco is usually my go-to bubble for large crowds, but there are many extremely well-made examples beyond Champagne.” Cava, Corpinnat, and Crémant are great options for large events.
  • DIY labels: If you don’t care about guests name-checking the bottles, consider customizing your own labels (with your initials or a sentimental illustration) and adhering them to the bottles.

The Best Wines for a Wedding

Surefire Crowd Pleasers

Matthew Jacobson, head sommelier at Vancouver’s Fairmont Pacific Rim, recommends keeping things simple at large events. “I try not to lean too far into the esoteric,” he says. “Don’t go too sweet, too spicy, or too acidic. Try to stick to tried and true styles, made in traditional ways.”

For whites, Jacobson recommends the following crowd-pleasers: Chablis, Sancerre, and Pinot Grigio. For reds, he opts for Etna Rosso for a Pinot-adjacent budget pick, but also enjoys classics like Nebbiolo, Chianti, Bordeaux, and California Cabs. 

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Cantina Terlano 2024 Tradition Pinot Bianco Pinot Bianco (Alto Adige)

Baked apples and fresh pears mingling with lemon curd like a pastry chef’s morning prep, everything rich but precisely measured. The palate keeps that balance between power and grace, candied citrus and warm bread notes flowing with the confidence of a winery that’s been mastering this dance since forever. Editors’ Choice. 93 Points — Jeff Porter

$24 Wine.come

CheckMate 2022 Fool’s Mate Chardonnay (Okanagan Valley)

Kick back and enjoy these orchard aromas of nectarines and yellow apples, not to mention wisps of toasted filberts and chamomile flowers. The wine’s modest acidity combines with a creamy texture and a bit of body to create a sinfully smooth sipping experience. The flavors of key lime pie, shortbread and lemon verbena tea are equally decadent. 92 Points — Michael Alberty

$87 Saratoga Wine

Tenuta delle Terre Nere 2024 Etna DOC Rosso Nerello Mascalese (Etna Rosso)

A cool, fresh nose offers aromas of blackberries, black plums, pepper and earth. Flavors of sweet blackberry jam and warm citrus headline the palate, before a dark chocolate ganache element takes over on the finish, lifted by flakes of salt but also reined in by tannins. 95 Points — Danielle Callegari

$31 Wine.com

Champagne

If you have a budget for higher-end bubbles, Auge recommends the gold standard. “I firmly believe that an occasion as important as a wedding deserves real Champagne,” she says.

And while larger Champagne houses have name recognition that can impress guests, Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Aleks Zecevic would opt for “grower” bottles, a type of Champagne in which the winemakers grow their own grapes.

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Louis Roederer 2018 Starck Brut Nature Blanc Champagne Blend (Champagne)

This expression embodies grace, with aromas of fresh pear, white peach, jasmine and violet framed by a subtle vein of pulverized seashell and chalk. The palate is guided by mouthwatering acidity and fine mousse, carrying citrus oils and crushed stone with quiet precision into a long, elegant finish. Proper aeration allows the mineral edges to open fully, delivering an irresistible and finely tuned sip. Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — Anna-Christina Cabrales

$110 Millesima

Krug NV Grande Cuvée 173ème Édition Brut Champagne Blend (Champagne)

The nose is immediately inviting, filled with toasted brioche topped with baked apple, pear and citrus peel, soft florals and spice for depth. The palate is generous and finely textured, balancing bright acidity with a creamy mousse that carries lemon confit, honeyed stone fruit enveloped in a nutty pastry. It finishes long, saline and utterly compelling, leaving a lasting impression of finesse and energy. Editors’ Choice. 96 Points — A.C.C.

$272 Wine.com

Charles Heidsieck NV Champagne Charlie Cellared in 2020 Champagne Blend (Champagne)

Captivating aromas of white peach and green apple unfold into wildflowers, light toffee, macadamia and a delicate mineral vein. The palate is precise, with poised orchard fruit that gains weight and intensity with aeration. A subtle toasty layer emerges adding depth, while bright acidity carries a long, chalky finish. Approachable with a brief decant, yet built to age. Ideal alongside butter-poached lobster to showcase its richness. Cellar Selection. 98 Points — A.C.C.

$580 Keg N Bottle

Italian Bubbles

If you’re set on serving bubbly but are worried about budget, Italian bubbles may be your new best friend. WE Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter says they are the perfect tool for navigating that price-quality balance.

“I feel that metodo classico wines offer great value and quality,” he says. “From Italy, you can find Franciacorta, Alta Langa, or Trento DOC. All three are great wines made like Champagne but not as expensive.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Ca’ del Bosco MV Cuvée Prestige 48 Edizione Extra Brut Sparkling Blend (Franciacorta)

This is the calling card and it earns that title with every sip. Baked bread, roasted pear, warmed honey and toasted nuts layered over a core of real depth and energy that sets the stage and raises the bar in the same breath. Full bodied and built to last, it moves with the ease and authority of something that has been done many times and perfected along the way. Close your eyes and you are already somewhere far more interesting than here. 94 Points — J.P.

$38 Zachys

Ettore Germano 2017 pas dosè Blanc de Blanc Chardonnay (Alta Langa)

This wine took eight years to arrive and carries every one of them with complete assurance. It opens like a Hollywood starlet on the red carpet, poised and dressed to kill, baked apples, lemon curd, fresh bread and pressed yellow and white flowers commanding the room with effortless authority. The palate is equally composed, a creamy rounded texture balanced by bright acidity while lemon cream, roasted almond and a long salty finish ensure the exit is just as memorable as the entrance. Drink now through 2035. Cellar Selection. 96 Points — J.P.

$90 Vintage Wine Merchants

Ferrari 2015 Lunelli Riserva Extra Brut Chardonnay (Trento)

Ground ginger and wildflowers swirl around warm, baking apples, creating a nose that’s both cozy and fresh. A pop of zippy lemon follows, with a punchy hit of tart lemon curd adding a crisp edge. This wine plays between warmth and zing, keeping each sip lively and irresistibly drinkable, yet time in the cellar will do magic. Drink Now – 2040. Cellar Selection. 98 Points — J.P.

$100 Wine Express

Albariño 

Albariño is “light, crispy, damn good, and most importantly, you can drink it all night long without getting bored,” says John Burns Paterson, who oversees the Nashville outpost of the NYC stalwart, Frankies Spuntino. “To me, that’s the key to a good wedding wine. Not to mention, it’ll pair with just about any setting.”

Beyond Albariño, Paterson keeps his options simple: one sparkling, one white, and one red. “There is no need to overcomplicate,” he adds. “At the end of the day, the guests just want to celebrate and have a good time.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Mar de Frades 2023 Albariño Albariño (Rías Baixas)

Enticing aromas of grapefruit rind and orange blossom give way to subtle hints of green pepper and white flowers. A pleasing saline character runs throughout, though the finish leans a touch too astringent, leaving the balance ever so slightly askew. 90 Points — Brandon Borcoman

$23 Harrison Wine Vault

Klinker Brick Winery 2024 Albariño (Mokelumne River)

This wine is another excellent example of aromatic white wine produced in an under-the-radar region. If you are an Albarino lover, this wine should be in your glass. It is fresh and zesty with aromas of green papaya, kiwi, and citrus, and notes of sweet basil leaves and vetiver on the nose; the flavors on the palate are high energy, Persian lime, White grapefruit, layered with White pepper, sedimentary rock, and a supple dry finish. pair with fried smelts. Best Buy. 93 Points — Tonya Pitts

$13 Empire Wine

Pinot Blanc

“Pinot Blanc is an easy-drinking, refreshing dry wine with a great balance of ripeness and freshness,” says Faucheaux. “It’s a great alternative to Pinot Grigio, which is fairly familiar to everyone.”

He recommends looking for bottles of Blanc from Alsace, France, in particular. “Some wines can be polarizing for people—too floral, too sweet, too savory or herbaceous,” he says. “But this wine is easy and versatile, subtle and elegant, and it’s honestly a crowd pleaser.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Trimbach 2023 Pinot Blanc Pinot Blanc (Alsace)

Classic and cleanly expressed, showing a crisp mix of apple and Meyer lemon with subtle floral accents. The palate is fresh and well balanced, supported by bright acidity that keeps the wine lively. Straightforward yet polished, finishing with good clarity and poise. 89 Points — Aleks Zecevic

$14 Empire Wines

Castel Sallegg 2023 Leopoldine Pinot Blanc (Alto Adige)

This captures that perfect moment when seasons collide. Magnolia blooms and preserved peaches bask in late summer warmth until mountain herbs and bright citrus announce change is coming. The palate masters the same balancing act, luxurious texture finding harmony with vibrant acidity. A wine that shows how contrast creates beauty. Drink Now – 2045 Editors’ Choice. 95 Points — J.P.

$26 Castel Sallegg

J. Lohr Vineyards & Wines 2023 F&G Vineyard Pinot Blanc (Arroyo Seco)

Pinot Blanc remains a rare standalone grape in California, and this bottling calls that infrequent starring role into question. Rounded aromas of melon, mint and chalk lead from the nose into a firmly structured palate exuberant in apple, pear and lime flavors. Refreshing but with ample body. Editors’ Choice. 91 Points — Matt Kettmann

Inquire with the winery

Verdicchio

Kindred is keen on Verdicchio, a crisp white from the Marche region of Italy. “[Verdicchio is] so delicious and shockingly inexpensive for the quality,” she says. “It’s clean, bright, with a little salinity (thanks to the proximity to the Adriatic Sea) that makes it both refreshing and a bit textured.”

Wine Enthusiast recommends:

Bucci 2021 Villa Bucci Riserva Verdicchio (Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico)

Here’s why Italian white wine deserves your cellar’s best real estate: green apple skin and Asian pear meet Meyer lemon with the kind of precision that defines greatness. Fresh herbs and stone notes build a framework for complexity that keeps revealing itself, sip after sip. The palate delivers profound depth without showing off, this is white wine operating at its highest level, as compelling now with dover sole as it will be in 2045 and beyond. Cellar Selection. 97 Points — J.P.

$110 Flatiron Wines & Spirits

Umani Ronchi 2022 Vecchie Vigne Verdicchio (Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico Superiore)

A faint, zesty lift of fresh citrus oil sets the stage for an explosion of orchard fruits, crisp Macintosh apples and sweet Seckel pears. The flavors come alive with preserved lemon and a salty, mineral edge, like licking a rock. Tart, electric acidity keeps it zippy and refreshing, making this Verdicchio both lively and energetic. 94 Points — J.P.

title: This French Region Is Making World-Class Pinot Without the Burgundy Price Tags
summary:
For the past several decades, Alsace has been defined by its white wines. Pinot Noir might change that.

The post This French Region Is Making World-Class Pinot Without the Burgundy Price Tags appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
With its tall bottles and aromatic whites, Alsace wine has been easy to pigeonhole. An outlier in France, often feeling closer in structure to Germany than to its home country, the region is known for winemaking that combines German precision with French finesse. And for the past several decades, at least, Alsace has been defined by its white wines, while reds remained a sidebar.

But something has shifted, under the radar. Without the marketing muscle of Burgundy or the rising buzz of German Spätburgunder, Pinot Noir in Alsace has gotten not just better, but serious. In fact, certain bottles would make you recalibrate what you thought you knew about the region.

“The quality of Alsatian Pinot Noir has been improving for 30 years, with a clear acceleration in the last decade,” says Maxime Barmès of Domaine Barmès-Buecher.

The easy explanation is climate change. Warmer vintages, better ripening, and more color and structure have impacted the wines’ character. But talk to growers, and that narrative starts to unravel. “Global warming can help ripening,” Barmès says, “but in very sunny years, it can also reduce aromatic finesse.”

Foulques Aulagnon, export marketing manager of CIVA (Alsace Wine Board), is more direct: “It is a revival, not an evolution.”

The Long, Twisty History of Alsatian Pinot Noir

Pinot Noir isn’t new to Alsace. During the Holy Roman Empire, the region built its reputation for red wines made from grapes grown in limestone, granite, and marl soils. That history was disrupted by the Thirty Years’ War, after which Alsace was repopulated under Louis XIII and XIV.

“These new farmer families came from Switzerland, Austria, and Germany, and had no tradition of producing serious red wine,” says Aulagnon.

What followed was a long decline. Under the German Empire, Alsace became a source of inexpensive wine. Pinot Noir was pushed to high yields, so the wines lost concentration and were reduced to something thin and simple. By the 1970s, the variety was barely relevant.

Then, came the revival. 

It didn’t begin in the vineyard, but in the classroom. In the 1970s, a new generation of Alsatian winemakers started looking toward Dijon’s Université de Bourgogne rather than Geisenheim’s Hochschule Geisenheim University. Burgundy became the reference point.

“Figures like Pierre Trimbach and René Muré brought back not just techniques, but a different philosophy: lower yields, élevage in oak, longer macerations, site expression,” says Aulagnon.

At estates like Domaine Albert Mann, this shift was decisive. In 1962, Pinot Noir accounted for just 1% of Alsace’s vineyard. Throughout the ‘60s and ‘70s, however, the Barthelmé family (who runs the domaine) began planting it on their best sites, including Hengst and Pfersigberg, and rethinking it entirely.

“Before climate change, there was a change of vision,” says Antoine Barthelmé. “We stopped treating Pinot Noir like a white wine.”

By the late 1980s, terroir-driven Pinot Noir had been reintroduced in Alsace. A second wave followed, with winemakers like Mélanie Pfister and Felix Meyer traveling beyond Burgundy, absorbing global ideas, and refining them back home.

The New Way

In the vineyard, the changes have been just as important. Instead of relying on high-yielding clones, many growers have shifted toward massal selection.

“It’s the mixture that contributes to the complexity in a plot, not a single phenotype,” says Barmès.

These selections tend to produce smaller berries, looser clusters, and more concentration, while diversifying vineyard plantings.

Viticulture has evolved, too. Lower yields are now the norm, often in the range of 30 to 35 hectoliters per hectare. Organic and biodynamic farming has become increasingly central. “Biodynamics naturally regulates yields, brings more depth, and improves the texture of Pinot Noir,” says Barthelmé.

Where Pinot Noir works best in Alsace is still an open question. Clay and marl bring structure and intensity to the wines, while those made in grapes grown in granite lean toward freshness.

“Pinot Noir can express itself on all types of Alsatian soils, as long as the work is done well,” Barmès says.

Barthelmé is more definitive. “There is no debate,” he says. “The matrix of Pinot Noir is limestone.”

In Pursuit of Precision

In the cellar, the shift has been toward restraint. Extraction is gentler, and oak is used more carefully. At some estates, like Barmès-Buecher, Pinot Noir is fully destemmed, with light punch-downs and aging in older barrels. The goal is precision, “to preserve the finesse of the Pinot Noir,” says Barmès.

At other estates, like Albert Mann, the approach is more flexible. Whole cluster fermentation can range from zero to 50 percent or more, while new oak is used sparingly. Barthelmé describes it as an “infusion mindset,” where the role of the winemaker is less to impose than to guide.

A growing number of winemakers are also pursuing a natural style. Christoph Binner and Catherine Riss show how minimal intervention can allow the grape to shine. The result is not a single expression, but a category in motion: Alsace Pinot Noir can be lifted and perfumed or deeper and more structured, depending on site and approach. What unites the best examples is balance.

Alsace is still often compared to Burgundy, if only because consumers need a reference point. But the gap is narrowing. “If you blind taste a great Alsace Pinot and a great Burgundy, Alsace has a good chance of competing with wines ten times more expensive,” says Barmès.

Barthelmé is less interested in comparison. “The future is not about creating a new style, but about being more precise.”

Pinot Noir now accounts for roughly 13% of Alsace’s plantings, up from just 8% in 2008. The growth is steady but measured, with increasing focus on the right sites.

For a region long defined by its whites, that might be the most telling sign of all. Alsace is refining something that was long underestimated.

Bottles to Try

Domaine Muré 2023 Clos Saint Landelin Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Classic and refined, showing a beautifully composed mix of cherry, violet, light licorice root, and subtle sandalwood. The palate is ripe and poised, medium to full in body yet never heavy, with polished tannins and well-integrated acidity providing lift. Elegant, balanced, and quietly powerful, it unfurls with grace into a long, harmonious finish. 93 Points — A.Z.

$63 Domaine Muré

Domaine Sipp-Mack 2023 Pinot Noir Vieilles Vignes Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Very pure and finely detailed, offering a beautiful aromatic mix of rosehip, hibiscus tea, and subtle rooibos. The palate is poised and graceful, with tannins that provide structure yet settle gently, never intruding on the fruit. Balanced and precise, this is a beautifully made Pinot Noir that combines delicacy with quiet depth and polish. Best Buy. 92 Points — A.Z.

$18 Boutique Vini

Trimbach 2023 Réserve Pinot Noir (Alsace)

Pure and finely detailed, showing violet, pomegranate, and rose with admirable clarity. The palate is supple and precise, with melting tannins that provide gentle support before fading seamlessly away. Fresh acidity keeps everything lifted, leaving a mouthwatering, elegant finish that underscores the wine’s poise and balance. 91 Points — A.Z.

title: Why Is It So Hard to Find Filipino Wine in the Philippines?
summary:
The Philippines has some of the best-tasting fruit in the world. So why is local wine so hard to come by?

The post Why Is It So Hard to Find Filipino Wine in the Philippines? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
How hard can it be to find Filipino wine in the Philippines? Turns out, the task isn’t as straightforward as it sounds.

Picture the world’s renowned wine-producing regions. Your first thought likely isn’t this Southeast Asian nation made up of thousands of islands. But there’s an inherent natural abundance in the Philippines, a country of mountains, coasts, volcanoes, and jungles. A plethora of fruits—calamansi, banana, mango, pineapple—thrive in its tropical climate. For centuries, produce here has been fermented into tasty beverages, such as basi, a fermented sugarcane wine, and tapuey, a rice wine, to which some Filipinos remain deeply attached.

Local companies like Proudly Promdi are leading the charge in rebranding and popularizing regional drinks as a source of pride. However, even with increased demand, these bottles can be difficult to track down.

Ahead of my 14-hour flight from Seattle to Manila, I drooled over Instagram posts featuring creative cocktails like the Basi Spritz and the Tapuey Negroni. As a first-time visitor to the Philippines, I wanted to sample drinks that I couldn’t make at home.

Proudly Promdi’s tagline touts that they are “rediscovering and celebrating Filipino heritage through artisanal spirits.” Promdi is slang for “from the province,” referring to the rural areas outside Manila, the bustling capital city home to around two million people. While it’s often used as a derogatory term, Proudly Promdi founder Ken Alonso, 39, is reclaiming the word—and the nation’s local wines and spirits.

Take tapuey. It’s made out of glutinous rice, a regional crop. Alonso explained that different varieties, including black, red, white, and brown, each produce their own distinctive taste. “Since we’re an archipelagic country, and we’re so scattered, each region or island will also have different interpretations of a different Filipino spirit,” he told me.

“We use a lot of tropical ingredients,” he said. “We in the Philippines arguably have the best-tasting fruits in the world: the sweetest ones, the juiciest ones.”

Unlike traditional dry grape wines, the fruit wines (which people also refer to as spirits) lean on the sweeter side, Alonso said. Sugar supports the fermentation process, as “these are fermented spirits only and not distilled spirits,” he added. “That’s actually very unique.”

On the morning of the Lunar New Year in February, I was on the hunt for Filipino wine and sunscreen. A local directed my fiancé and me down the Taytay-El Nido National Highway to a convenience store crowded with early birds in the figurative sense (shoppers) and the literal sense (chickens).

We scanned the glass case and snatched up the last bottle of precious SPF. I asked the shopkeeper, “Do you know where I can find wine here, po?” (The Tagalog word po is a sign of respect.)

“White or red?” he said, to which I countered, “Sugarcane or coconut, please.” He pointed me to the back of his shop, and I squeezed between the shelves of rum, gin, mojito mix … wine!

The front of the bottle featured a red label with a muscular man lifting a tiger and the brand name, Ursus Wine, in bold letters. And in the corner of the label: Made in the Philippines. This must be it. A man wiped down the dusty bottle before taking our cash.

But my sense of triumph wouldn’t last long. I noticed a passerby recoil at the sight of my purchase. Upon further investigation, it was determined to be a Chinese-style herbal wine. The search continued.

Alonso wasn’t surprised at the hurdles I faced as a tourist in hot pursuit of Filipino wines. Visitors are typically offered French wine or American whiskey, not tubâ, a coconut wine, and other island offerings. He said that’s based on a widespread cultural misbelief that Filipino wines aren’t up to snuff. This thinking is a product of the aftershock of colonization. Spain, the U.S., and Japan each took turns occupying the Philippines, which finally gained independence in 1946.

Alonso confided that he only discovered some local drinks later in life. The first time he drank tapuey was at his aunt’s 50th wedding anniversary in 2011. Even as a local, “we didn’t know that we had so many Filipino spirits,” he said.

My quest resumed on the streets of El Nido. Young students on mopeds zoomed to school, and workers corralled sightseers onto beaches for boat tours. As we wandered past one of the many nondescript shops, rows of liquor bottles caught my eye.

After a furtive glance at the shelves, I resigned myself to another defeat when I did a double take: three boxes of Vigan Basi sugarcane wine tucked in the top corner. They cost 500 pisos, or about $9—jackpot.

Back at the bungalow, I let the bottle chill in the mini fridge for about an hour before pouring the cognac-brown wine into a glass. The aroma was potently sweet like that of its distilled cousin, rum. The flavor was strong and tangy, with smooth, earthy undertones. With each passing minute, it grew on me. It was only one variation of local wine, but it tasted like success.

For the rest of the vacation, I resigned myself to the same old cocktails slung by bartenders near and far. Filipino wines largely remain my white whale, swimming in the waters of the South China Sea. Maybe, one day, my thirst will be quenched.

title: Italian Wine Has a Secret Weapon (Hint: It’s Italy)
summary:
At Wine Enthusiast's third-annual Sip of Italy, experts discussed the passion, terroir, and indigenous varieties that makes Italian wine so unique.

The post Italian Wine Has a Secret Weapon (Hint: It’s Italy) appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Italian wine hardly needs a sales pitch. But like everywhere in the wine world, Italian pros are grappling with how best to set the industry up for success amid changing consumer tastes, a warming climate, and a tumultuous economic landscape—all while enjoying what we love about Italian wine in the first place.

“Italy is a state of mind. That’s the secret,” says Salvatore Napolitano, executive managing director of Terlato‘s Italian portfolio. At the end of the day, he argues, we need to remember what Italian culture represents—“conviviality, sharing, engaging people of different backgrounds and sensibilities”—because “wine is a conduit for it.” 

On September 14 at City Winery in New York City, Wine Enthusiast held its third-annual Sip of Italy event. With a trade portion that featured a panel of Italian wine experts, as well as a walkaround tasting with bottles from over 100 producers poured, the event was a lively summit on the future of Italy’s dynamic wine scene. 

Here’s what we took away from it.

Let Italy be Italy.

WE Writer-at-Large Jeff Porter opened the panel by acknowledging that, more than anything else, Italian wine stands for “passion” and “conviviality.” This theme came up repeatedly, both in the trade panel and on the tasting floor, as pros court a new generation of drinkers who are less impressed with pedigree and more drawn to experiences.

Napolitano argues that the country’s lack of a cohesive, singular voice, due to its relatively recent unification, is part of what makes the wine scene so special and “democratic.” The other part is the land—and the special relationship Italians have with it.

“Geologically speaking, we have one of the most unique terroirs in the world,” he says. “We are great farmers because we speak to the land.” 

As Michael Duffy, sommelier and wine director at Daniel Humm’s forthcoming restaurant, Humm, puts it: “Italy needs to let itself be Italy.” Wine professionals should remember that, in Italy, “wine is food,” he says. “Whether the wine you’re drinking is a $20 Gaglioppo or a storied bottle from the cellar that’s worth thousands.”

‘Less-famous’ regions are the future.

Duffy predicts that the lesser-known Italian wine regions—Alto Adige, Valle d’Aosta, Southern Italy—are “the new frontier.”

“Due to several factors, climate change being an inevitable factor… we’re going to have to start looking to new-to-some places where great wines are going to be grown and made,” he says.  

The same is true for grape varietals. Italy is a land of countless indigenous grapes, most of which are largely unknown to international consumers. That doesn’t mean the consumer isn’t interested. When Duffy was the wine director at New York’s acclaimed Italian restaurant Rezdora, he decided not to pour international varieties by the glass. “We can’t just respond to the market,” he says. “We have to create the market where [it doesn’t] exist.”

Italian food is made for Italian wine.

That seems like a simple sentiment, but it may be the key to telling the story of just how spectacular Italian wine really is.

Michael Laudenslager, a Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large who reviews wines from Tuscany, Southern Italy, and Sardinia, thinks that the key to marketing lesser-known Italian wines, both in retail and at restaurants, is to highlight the foods made in those same regions. Think Ligurian wines and pesto, Campanian wines and Bufala mozzarella, etc.

“There should be a shift towards wine as a part of everyday life, like it’s food,” says Valerie Pimpinelli, general manager and buyer for Flatiron Wines & Spirits. “Taking the pretension out is the number one thing.”

The consumer isn’t stupid.

For the industry to succeed, wine needs to feel more accessible and less intimidating. But that shouldn’t come at the expense of detailed storytelling.

“A cultural trend we should all fight is the TL:DR-ification of everything,” says Duffy. “It’s this idea that people don’t want to engage with a serious book or a long story. That’s thinking the consumer is stupid.”

That doesn’t mean, however, that they necessarily want to hear about hyper-technical production methods of wine when they’re choosing a bottle at the store. “People don’t care about the pH or size of barrels,” says Pimpinelli frankly. “It almost diminishes the pleasure.”

Bottled wine cocktails are hot.

On the tasting floor, product innovation was on full display, as many producers lean into consumer taste for wine cocktails. Brightly colored bottles of ready-to-drink mimosas, bellinis, and spritzes littered the tables, while trays of mimosas floated around the room.

These drinks tend to be much lower in abv than regular wine, typically hovering around 4 to 7%, which makes them attractive to the growing contingent of drinkers searching for lower-proof options. They also lean on the sweeter side, making them an ideal choice for an aperitif.

In Italy, “aperitivo is part of the culture,” says Porter. “Now, producers are making it even more accessible by having them in the RTDs. We’ve seen that in the grocery stores in Italy, and now we’re seeing it more here.”

The Canella Family, pioneers of RTD wine cocktails who have been making their bottled bellinis since 1988, have recently begun making a special bottling specifically for Costco’s Kirkland brand. Alvise Canella, the third-generation Canella who works alongside his brother to oversee production, believes their success can be partly attributed to the simple ingredients in their products. They contain no added sugars, relying on the fruits’ natural sugars instead, and they opt to preserve through pasteurization as opposed to using dangerous additives.

Elsewhere in the tasting room, importers showed off a classic limoncello spritz and Casa Cipriani’s beloved bellini in RTD form. They spoke of success across the United States and abroad, and they hinted at smaller formats (187 mls) making a splash in the future.

title: This Wine-Filled Australian City Doesn’t Care If You Think It’s Boring
summary:
There are two types of Canberrans: those who will “fight tooth and nail” to prove their city isn’t boring, and those happy for outsiders to keep believing it.

The post This Wine-Filled Australian City Doesn’t Care If You Think It’s Boring appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
My kids are lovely, but they are still kids, which means they wait all of one minute after I return from a trip to ask, “What did you get us?” 

So, on my first day in Canberra, Australia, I did something uncharacteristically strategic with a pocket of free time: I shopped for local gifts instead of panic-buying two comically large Toblerone bars and a bag of Haribo gummy bears—the universal peace offering of the procrastinating traveler.

At POP, a boutique showcasing goods from more than 300 local makers on Braddon’s restaurant- and shop-lined Lonsdale Street, I paused at a rack of colorful magnets. Amid the clever illustrations and local landmarks, one theme kept appearing: “Keep Canberra Boring.” 

Hardly a confidence-inspiring welcome on day one.

The modern city of Canberra was designed as a capital before it had a chance to decide whether it wanted to be anything else. In 1912, Australia selected the winning plan created by American architectural partners Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin. From Mount Ainslie Lookout, the geography—and geometry—is impossible to miss: the Australian War Memorial and Parliament House face each other across Lake Burley Griffin along the city’s land axis. It is beautiful, no doubt. But it is also visibly engineered—not exactly helpful to a capital often reduced to politicians, public servants, and school excursions. 

Andrew Ly knew little about that reputation when he moved from Toronto with his partner, Jennaya Montgomery. What surprised him was how often locals raised the diss themselves. 

“People kept bringing it up,” he says. “Colleagues, friends and people we met would go out of their way to tell me that Canberra was actually exciting, or to point out all the things that made it a great place to live.” Ly and Montgomery eventually turned that defensiveness into a playground-style comeback through their design company, North/South: “Canberra Thinks You’re Boring Too.”

The slogan caught on because it spoke to two kinds of Canberrans, Ly explains: those who will “fight tooth and nail” to prove their city isn’t boring, and those happy for outsiders to keep believing it. Fewer visitors mean less traffic and shorter lines, right?

A similar instinct to question an assumption and then test it also shaped the Canberra District, a wine region straddling the Australian Capital Territory and neighboring New South Wales. As we drove the Barton Highway toward Murrumbateman, ordered suburbs gave way to sheep paddocks and flashes of parrots. En route, Laura Jallier, owner of local wine tour company Van Du Vin, described the region to me: “It’s got a nerdy, cool vibe. But I mean ‘nerdy’ in an Australian way, which is actually a really nice way to say it.” 

The Scientists Who Planted Anyway

That vibe has institutional roots. In the postwar decades, Canberra drew researchers to institutions such as the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Australia’s national science agency. Among them were biochemist and physicist John Kirk, insect ecologist Ken Helm, and entomologist Edgar Riek, who planted vines in the surrounding sheep country in the early 1970s. They had come to Canberra as researchers, not winemakers.

“People thought we were mad: ‘Canberra? It’s too bloody cold! You can’t grow grapes there,’” recalls Helm. But these researchers had something would-be vignerons seldom have: salaried day jobs. Those secure jobs—Canberra’s “golden handcuffs,” as Jallier calls them—allowed them to pay the bills while their fledgling wine businesses developed. The lack of a modern wine tradition also gave them room to tinker. “They didn’t listen because they are scientists,” says Jallier. 

Helm and his wife, Judith, established Helm Wines in 1973. Today, he pours Riesling—including an unusual but incredibly delicious Riesling Rosé—and Cabernet Sauvignon in an 1888 schoolhouse he moved to the property by truck. The building had also once served as a temperance hall. “They’re all turning in their graves now,” he says.

 Members of the Canberra wine community are rarely restrained by historical precedents. Stephanie Helm, Ken and Judith’s daughter and the winemaker behind The Vintner’s Daughter, describes a wine region born from “inquiring minds”—people asking what would happen if they planted grapes in Canberra or tried a different clone. “It’s never, ‘Just do it as we always would,’” she says. “It’s always, ‘What’s new? What can we try?’”

Shiraz, But Make It Pinot

In 1971, John Kirk planted Clonakilla’s first vines on land previously used to raise sheep for fine wool. His son, Tim Kirk, now the winery’s chief winemaker, sees a direct connection. The cool, moderately fertile conditions that make sheep grow low-micron wool—the kind used for quality suits—also suited fine-wine grapes. 

Clonakilla’s Shiraz Viognier is a striking counterpoint to the fuller-bodied, plush reds many Americans associate with Australia. Kirk describes it as medium-bodied and leaning “more in the Pinot direction.” 

His approach is at once earnest and irreverent. “When you put Shiraz in these soils, in this climate, and your viticulture is careful and loving and attentive, you can produce amazingly good fruit,” he says. Then, the winemaker’s task is simple: “Don’t bugger up the fruit.” 

For many U.S. drinkers, Canberra’s Shiraz may be the clearest path into the region. Kathy Marlin, senior vice president of sales for Clonakilla’s U.S. importer, Winebow, says buyers expecting Barossa Shiraz’s brambly black fruit and heft find something else in Clonakilla: fine red fruit, cracked pepper, and freshness. The larger obstacle is recognition. “The general consumer still sees Australia as one offer, one style,” she says. 

Riesling from the region can be similarly distinctive. Emma Shaw, a local winemaker who runs the Canberra Cellar Door pop-up at the Canberra and Region Visitors Centre, describes them as floral and green-apple bright, with “manic acidity” that “melts” across the palate. I tasted that as an electric freshness that softened into an almost creamy finish. 

At Rizla, Australia’s only Riesling-focused wine bar, local bottlings presented an embarrassment of riches. Parmesan fries, sticky pork loin, and charred broccolini somehow all seemed made for every selection on the list.

Exclusive Access to
Wine Country,
Led by Wine Enthusiast

More than half a century after Canberra’s modern wine founders planted their first vines, Shiraz and Riesling may have emerged as regional calling cards, but producers are still more keen to experiment than get boxed into a certain way of doing things. Stephanie, who made her first wine at nine, uses Babydoll sheep short enough to graze beneath the vines; her young son, home sick from school that day, tagged along happily as she showed them to me. 

At Ravensworth, former chef Bryan Martin ferments wine in concrete tanks, ceramic amphorae, and glass globes, which together look more like the lab of a mad scientist than a traditional cellar. “We cold-stabilize the whites and dry-age the beef at the same time,” he said of a cold room they had built. 

Mount Majura Vineyard grows everything from Tempranillo and Touriga Nacional to Mencía, Albariño, and Mondeuse. “We do small batches and we muck around,” says sales and marketing manager Fergus McGhie.

Beyond the Cellar Door

That same precision and playfulness followed me back to the city. At Canberra Glassworks, a patient, passionate artist helped me make a glass bird—my youngest son’s nickname—in furnace heat that I had badly underestimated when I chose to wear a cashmere sweater that morning. 

At Lunetta Trattoria, over the best roast chicken of my life, I watched a bartender run a lemon rind around a glass rim with enormous care. When one bartender gently corrected another’s technique, it felt like mutual investment in getting the task right. 

Floating Sauna on Lake Burley Griffin, which had opened only months before my visit, offered another change in perspective. What had looked like pure geometry from Mount Ainslie felt elemental at water level: wood-fired heat, cold lake, and a peaceful, tree-lined shore. I sweated, plunged into the cold lake, and repeated the cycle, emerging from the experience both deeply calm and weirdly energized. I was ready for a glass of Riesling.

From a distance, earnestness can seem boring. Up close, it feels like care.

By the time I left, “Canberra Thinks You’re Boring Too” no longer sounded only like a comeback. If boring meant chasing a question into a vineyard, fussing over a lemon rind, and still greeting a glass of wine—or a plunge into a cold lake—with childish wonder, perhaps it was also a compliment. Maybe Canberra thought I was boring, too. I hope so.

Turn the Ordinary Into Extraordinary with Covalli Prosecco

“Few sounds spark joy like the pop of a wine cork—especially when the bottle’s filled with something bubbly.”

Few sounds spark joy like the pop of a wine cork—especially when the bottle’s filled with something bubbly. With Covalli Prosecco, adding a shimmer to life’s every day moments just got a whole lot easier. Whether unwinding after a long day of work or gearing up for guests on the weekend, simply grab your favorite wine glass and let the wine do the rest.

Born in the rolling hills of Italy’s Veneto region, Covalli Prosecco brings the celebratory spirit synonymous with northern Italy straight to your home. Each bottle of Covalli Prosecco captures the unique Italian essence of dolce far niente—the sweetness of doing nothing—with its crisp, fruit-forward flavors and invigorating mousse. Produced in both brut and rosé styles, Covalli Prosecco’s diverse profiles speak to a variety of preferences and pairings, it’s simply a matter of taste.

Covalli Prosecco Brut is crafted entirely from the Glera grape. This lively and refreshing sparkler showcases signature flavors of green apple, citrus, and pear, with energizing acidity and a long finish. Its counterpart, Covalli Prosecco Rosé, incorporates a hint of Pinot Nero for color and flavor, resulting in a fruit-driven rosato with notes of raspberry, apple, white peach, and strawberry. Fresh and approachable, both wines are crafted with the utmost attention to detail, and are designed to enhance any moment where wine is enjoyed.

Covalli Prosecco makes savoring a glass of bubbly an attainable daily luxury, thanks to its accessible price point. As universally elevated prices continue to limit wine lovers’ access to high-quality bottles, Covalli Prosecco welcomes sparkling enthusiasts with exuberance and joy, ready to captivate and delight from the very first sip.

Beyond sipping solo, Covalli Prosecco equally shines in brunch cocktails and spritz recipes. The wine’s signature citrus notes perfectly complement freshly squeezed juices in mimosas, while its zesty acidity and bright, fruit-forwardness come to life when mixed with bittersweet aperitivi or elderflower liqueur in spritzes. And, Covalli Prosecco is just as adaptable on the table, pairing with everything from charcuterie boards and soft, creamy cheeses to seafood dishes, sushi, and fried appetizers. This innate versatility makes Covalli Prosecco an easy choice for effortless entertaining and everyday enjoyment. Simply pop the cork and let the bubbles do the rest!

title: A Longshot Canadian Wine Region Is Winning Over Skeptical Locals—and the World
summary:
After years of experimentation in Eastern Townships, skilled producers are turning hybrids and finicky Vitis vinifera into electric, elegant bottles.

The post A Longshot Canadian Wine Region Is Winning Over Skeptical Locals—and the World appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
A blizzard was coming, the sky grew dark, and Anne-Marie Lemire was remarkably unbothered.

“It’s been 25 years since we’ve had a storm like this,” said Lemire, the owner of Vignoble Courville in Quebec’s Eastern Townships. I stood in her warmly lit tasting room, peering out the windows, wondering if my boots were fully waterproof. (They weren’t.)

As flurries swirled over her 40 acres, Lemire told me how some winemakers in the region drape their vines in geothermal fabrics and intentionally bury them in the snow to protect them from harsher elements. It’s the sort of homegrown ingenuity that -30°F winters require.

“It’s a good day for vin chaud,” she said, and set a pot of mulled wine to warm on the stovetop. If there’s a better snapshot of the casual attitude and aspirational hardiness of Québécois winemaking, I haven’t found it.

Also known as Cantons de l’Est, the Eastern Townships is a startlingly beautiful wine region an hour or so east of Montreal near the Vermont border. If the name isn’t yet familiar, it’s because commercial viticulture here only began in the 1980s. Like all elder Millennials, it’s experienced seismic changes in those 40-odd years.

Most of the developments are positive. Amid an ever-shifting climate, farming and winemaking practices have evolved and improved. After years of experimentation, skilled producers are now able to turn hybrids and finicky Vitis vinifera into electric, elegant bottles that impress skeptical locals and international critics. You’ll see them on the lists of the coolest wine bars and restaurants in Montreal, not to mention in Toronto, New York, and beyond.

All of this makes for an especially meaningful time for Eastern Townships wine. With fresh momentum and buzzy interest near and far, what happens next feels poignant. Can this patchwork of fiercely independent producers come together to codify their wine scene and compete on a global stage? Do they even want to?

One of the first wineries to showcase the region’s potential was Les Pervenches, a 10-acre, small-production family operation near Farnham. Home to some of the oldest vinifera vines in Quebec, it’s helmed by Véronique Hupin and Mike Marrler, who have been certified organic since 2007 and biodynamic since 2008.

“We’re farmers first,” Hupin said as she poured me a glass of minerally, single-vineyard Chardonnay in her cozy tasting room on a far sunnier day.

I am lucky to try it; Les Pervenches’ vintages almost always sell out immediately. Most bottles go to club members and devoted somms and restaurateurs. In addition to that crisp, linear Chardonnay, their range includes a showstopping Pinot Noir, plus Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Zweigelt, and a blend of Chardonnay with Seyval Blanc, a hybrid white-wine grape bred in Wisconsin to withstand cold temperatures.

Seyval Blanc is one of several hybrid varieties that thrive in the Eastern Townships’ Nordic terroirs and tough winters. Some 80% of all wine grapes planted in Quebec are hybrids, with Frontenac Noir, Frontenac Blanc, and Vidal leading the pack. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are the most common vinifera, but they account for around 6% and 4% of all plantings, respectively.

“Here in Quebec, we used to always drink French and Italian wine, so it’s a big step to drink what is different and what is made here,” Lemire says. “People are accepting more and more that you can make quality wines with hybrids.”

It’s easy to see why. During the last 10 to 15 years, talented Eastern Townships winemakers have transformed the local wine scene. It’s no longer all about what Les Pervenches’ Marler calls “tourist wine,” or treacly bottlings geared toward travelers who primarily think of vineyards as photogenic backdrops for weddings.

Instead, a crop of independent producers has focused on how to ripen vinifera in their short growing season, and how to finesse the searing acidity and distinctive flavors of hybrid grapes. It’s a quality-minded, climate-resistant approach.

“Quebec winemakers are some of the best in the wine industry at managing climate change because we have had to manage a complicated environment since day one,” says Frédéric Simon, co-owner of the boutique winery Pinard et Filles. “For us, it’s not, are we going to get a spring frost? It’s when are we going to get a spring frost?”

I contemplated this existentialistic commitment to preparedness as I stood with Simon on his windswept 18.5 acres. In 2011, he and his co-founder and wife, Catherine Belanger, began sustainably farming the plot off a tree-lined road near Lake Memphremagog. Now in their 10th vintage, they grow some 24 varieties of hybrids and vinifera. Bottlings span an ethereal blanc de blancs, varietal Chardonnay, complex skin-contact wines, and crunchy red blends made with Gamay and Marquette, among others.

With limited production and chic labels designed by Montreal-based artist Marc Séguin, Pinard et Filles has garnered cult status in Quebec and beyond. A handful of bottles are exported to the United States by New York-based importer Zev Rovine Selections. “There’s this incredible amount of extra work it takes to do wine up there,” Rovine says. “It’s inspiring in one way, and head-scratching in another.”

Despite the mounting enthusiasm and recognition for their hard-won expertise, Eastern Townships winemakers still face a slew of misconceptions at home and abroad. “For an American or a European, when they think of Quebec, they think of Eskimos and igloos and winter,” Simon says. “They think that it’s so harsh living here and so cold. When we tell them that we’re making wine here, they’re like, ‘Wait, you make wine? What are you growing? Are you making wine with rhubarbs?’”

Without a rhubarb in sight, what does seem to be gaining ground in the Eastern Townships is sparkling wine production. Wineries like Le Domaine Bergeville in Hatley use hybrids and vinifera, or blends of both, to make complex, traditional-method bubbles.

“There’s unique tension and freshness to these wines,” says Joanie Métivier, the beverage director of Manoir Hovey, a resort in North Hatley. She credits this to winemakers learning how to balance the naturally high acidity of their grapes. “Because we have these very cold winters, people forget that we also have a beautiful growing season with very warm summers.”

Manoir Hovey is a Relais & Chateaux property whose fine-dining restaurant pairs tasting menus with local and world-famous wines, but where it’s also socially acceptable to wear ski pants to breakfast. Tourism here is on the upswing; Métivier has noticed more visitors coming to the Eastern Townships ever since the pandemic.

The local market is evolving, too. As tariffs continue to influence what people eat and drink, many Québécois are appreciative of the bounty in their backyards. “Fifteen years ago, when we started talking about making quality wine in Quebec, it seemed impossible to a lot of people,” Simon says. “Now, more and more people are interested in what we are trying to do.” Within the next decade, Eastern Townships wine “will get the global recognition that it deserves,” he predicts.

In the meantime, there’s an opportunity for area winemakers to define and classify their terroirs, Métivier says. It’s not a bid for increased governmental regulation, like the American Viticultural Area system that delineates Oak Knoll from Stags Leap in the Napa Valley. Instead, it’s an effort to highlight and sustain the momentum that winemakers here have worked so tirelessly to build.

“We’re not trying to make Napa wines or Bordeaux wines,” Métivier says. “We want to make Quebec wines.”

Carl Jung famously theorized that ideas surface simultaneously in unconnected minds, drawn from a shared reservoir he called the collective unconscious. Usually this theory is invoked to explain myths or creative phenomena. Lately it explains something that’s happening in what I’ll call the cocktail unconscious: the great re-awakening of Hpnotiq. You know, the vodka-based neon-blue liqueur popularized by the early 2000s hip-hop scene. 

For the uninitiated: Hpnotiq is a French liqueur made with tropical fruit juices (including mango and passion fruit), vodka, and a touch of cognac. It debuted in 2001, and within three years it went from roughly a thousand cases sold to over a million, thanks to word of mouth, a nightclub stunt involving an Incredible Hulk costume, and the legendary Master P lyric “My favorite drink is that Incredible Hulk (Uuuughhhh!).”

The Incredible Hulk, a lurid green Hennessy-Hpnotiq cocktail sure to give you a good time (and story to tell) became shorthand for a specific era of club culture. I will age myself here and admit that during Hpnotiq’s mid-aughts peak, I was a junior in high school. I should specify: I was a junior in high school in Miami, which means my first Incredible Hulk was purchased with a fake ID at a club. 

My palate couldn’t handle the bitterness of Hennessy back then, but sweet, fruity Hpnotiq was music to my mouth. The glitzy, psychedelic bottle became a must-have showpiece for a boat day. Hpnotiq was even in the room—or rather, the jacuzzi—the day I had sex for the first time. Clearly I have fond memories, and I’m not alone.

Lou Charbonneau, beverage director of Boston-based Xenia Greek Hospitality, smuggled Hpnotiq into his college dorm. “There were definitely Incredible Hulks being made, like, very crudely,” he says. “I should also add that it was a dry campus.” 

Fast forward to 2023, when Charbonneau threw a cyberpunk-themed Halloween party at Hecate, a bar in Boston’s Back Bay neighborhood and part of Xenia, where a regular night in its black-and-gold cave feels like descending into the underworld. For one night Charbonneau turned the space into a futuristic dive bar with neon lights, a frozen machine, and—you guessed it—a Hpnotiq cocktail.

“I wanted a tongue-in-cheek offering, to make it a fever dream for anyone who came in,” he says. “Everyone was so excited for Hpnotiq to be anywhere.” 

Afterward he couldn’t stop thinking about how to fold the liqueur beloved by nightclub-going party animals into Hecate’s high-concept menu, where every cocktail has a mythology and bartenders are “spirit guides.” 

He succeeded with Clarke’s Third Law, a drink containing mellowcorn, freeze-dried fassionola, acidified Pocari Sweat (a Japanese sports drink), powdered albumin (an essential protein found in human blood), and Hpnotiq to round it out. It’s named after Arthur C. Clarke’s notion that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic. 

While developing the drink for the Hecate party, Charbonneau recalls, “I kept asking what would be accessible and necessary in the future.” 

He landed on water, vitamins, electrolytes, corn, and Hpnotiq—it does have a blend of tropical fruits, after all. The Clarke’s Third Law was a smashing hit.

One mile away, connected in the cocktail unconscious, Eliza Hoar was also putting Hpnotiq on the menu at Equal Measure in Fenway, Boston. She and Charbonneau had been introduced by mutual friend Jay Giordano from the distillery Heaven Hill (the company would soon fold Hpnotiq into its portfolio—synchronicities abound!). 

The happy accident led to a match made in Hpnotiq: they drank it, took uncoordinated but nearly identical photos holding the radioactive-looking bottle in moody lighting at their respective venues, discovered each other’s photos, and joked about collectively championing the liqueur. 

You know what they say: in every joke there’s a spark of truth.

Where’s the Hpnotiq Party At?

Once Giordano started working for Heaven Hill, he did his part to champion it as well. “Jay got his hands on the photos Eliza and I took and shared them on Instagram. Everyone was like, is there a Hpnotiq party happening?” Charbonneau says. 

The response was overwhelming, though a few rolled their eyes. “The majority of bartenders scoff at Hpnotiq, but I don’t think we ought to scoff at anything,” he argues. “If we’re talking lowbrow or detested products, Malört fits in there too.” 

Rather than shy away, Charbonneau is leaning in. He uses Malört, a wormwood liqueur, to give structure and bitterness to Hpnotiq, a combination that has since appeared in his pop-ups nationwide. Bar Vlaha, also part of Xenia, serves Hpnotiq in a guava-and-dill swizzle with Ocho Plata and green Chartreuse. Hecate’s next menu will introduce the Moonchild, with Ocho tequila, lacto-fermented cherry soda, bitter Hpnotiq, and a Maillard chocolate air foam.

Meanwhile Hoar is holding down Hpnotiq on the West Coast. After moving to California to become the director of bars at Rosewood Miramar Beach in May 2025, she has wanted to sneak it onto the hotel’s Manor Bar menu, she says, “but not make an Incredible Hulk.” 

The self-proclaimed geek leaned into a literary theme, pulling from novels, screenplays, and lyrics that romanticize California. Her “California Love” is made with Grey Goose, Hpnotiq, lemon, and sparkling wine, served in a tulip-shaped glass adorned with a crystal bandana. It’s a flip on a French 75, Hoar explains, and an homage to Tupac’s Compton, his favorite drink, and the lyrics “one part Alizé, one part Cristal. Thug’s passion, baby.” 

This year, The Manor Bar joined the 50 Best Discovery List. Hoar is now at work on their next new menu, inspired by spies and meant to read like a case file. There will of course be a Vesper honoring Ian Fleming’s debut Bond novel, Casino Royale, but also, don’t be surprised to spot something Hpnotiq-blue.

A Neon Revolution

The cocktail unconscious continues to churn: At another luxe hotel nearby, Fairmont Breakers Long Beach, bartender Roberto Del Campo is hoping a different neon-colored liqueur gets its day in the sun. Enter the Midori Sour, only available for Monday industry nights at HALO Rooftop Bar. Suntory launched Midori (the Japanese word for green) in the U.S. market in 1978, with an exclusive debut at Studio 54 that coincided with a party for the Saturday Night Fever cast. The sweet liqueur ruled the disco era, only to become regarded as a cheap party trick in elite mixology circles. Its arc from punchline back to prestige remains to be seen. 

Jay Giordano put it best: “Some of [the change] has to do with the industry in general kind of lightening up. When people like Eliza and Lou, who are at the top of their game, play around in this way that’s still elevated, it inspires healthy competition in the younger generation.”

title: Are Reservation-Only Tasting Rooms Hurting Wineries?
summary:
Shifting to reservations helped tasting rooms stay afloat during the pandemic. With visitation down, that may be hurting wineries more than helping.

The post Are Reservation-Only Tasting Rooms Hurting Wineries? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Mandatory pandemic restrictions forced California wineries to switch to reservation systems, but post-lockdown demand has since fallen to 20-year lows.
  • Consumers miss spontaneous walk-ins, prompting many wineries to adopt flexible, hybrid models to boost foot traffic and sales.
  • Reservations enable personalized guest experiences, though local permit restrictions often dictate whether walk-ins are legally allowed.

In the early aughts, most California wineries operated on a drop-in basis. Guests could roll up to their favorite winery, sip through a line-up, enjoy the views, and then move on. 

When Covid-19 hit, that model fell out of favor for practical reasons, and wineries relied more on reservations to welcome in guests. These measures were helpful in facilitating social distancing and safer visitations. However, as restrictions were lifted, the reservation system stuck. 

Many winery teams argue that reservations create more intimate, customized experiences, while helping them save on staffing costs. But some consumers argue that, when tasting rooms require reservations, visiting them feels less welcoming, and removes any chance of spontaneity.

This debate is amplified by the fact that tasting room visits at U.S. wineries have not returned to pre-pandemic numbers. Demand has slumped, hitting a 20-year low.

As a result, some wineries are switching approaches. “You’re seeing a lot of sandwich boards in Napa Valley that say, we accept walk-ins,” says Vida DeLong, who runs Hopscotch DTC consulting.

So, what’s the right reservation model?

A Post-Covid Shake-Up

When businesses reopened after Covid-19 shutdowns, operators realized the reservation model came with myriad benefits. “It allowed better planning, an understanding of what was coming up,” says Jonathan Wendorf, director of consumer sales and marketing at Sequoia Grove Winery.

As post-lockdown tourism rebounded, sales were strong—until they weren’t. When, ostensibly, the excitement of getting back to wine country wore off, businesses began to scramble. “People are looking to take walk-ins—do everything that they can,” Wendorf says.

California’s J. Lohr Vineyards has switched from a reservations-only model to a reservations-encouraged model. “With traffic being down and guests expecting walk-in service again, we are able to accommodate both,” says Jessica Kolhoff, director of hospitality and direct sales. 

Sure, they have to be more reactive with staffing, entertaining a growing number of “custom” guest experiences. “There is an expectation for seated tastings, indoor versus outdoor options,  food, and special accommodations—kids, large parties, lingering visits, etc.,” says Kollhoff. “The expectation around the level of hospitality is also higher.”

With growing inflation and ever-rising tasting fees, can we blame consumers?

“With the increased fees associated with tastings valley-wide, tourists are, rightfully, expecting a more elevated experience than those that Napa was known for in its earlier days,” says Luke Jeramaz, digital marketing manager at Grgich Hills Estate. “They expect a degree of privacy, a peaceful setting, and a knowledgeable host that personalizes their experience.”

Grgich still embraces both reservations and walk-ins, but the split has changed. Pre-pandemic, 70% of guests were walk-in only. Now, 85% of guests book ahead of time. 

With its inherent need for more staff, this business model is no easy feat to maintain, but it does work. “Our wine educators maintain steady work hours, and our guests receive far more personalized, one-on-one experiences,” says Jeramaz. “The added expense is balanced out by the fact that we rarely have to turn away guests, leading to greater tasting room traffic and increased chances of conversions.”

Weighing What Customers Want 

DeLong has found the hybrid model is working well for her clients, primarily because what visitors want from the region has changed. 

“What we’re finding is that visitors [and] day-trippers want to just play it by ear and see where the day takes them,” she says. 

Many wineries have launched urban tasting rooms, capturing travelers who don’t want to spend an hour driving and finding parking in wine country, and for whom a $180, two-hour tasting doesn’t appeal. “They don’t need to drive, and they can hit six, seven, eight different tasting rooms in an afternoon with zero planning,” DeLong explains.

There’s also the saturation factor—Napa Valley has a large number of wineries to choose from (around 475, though not all offer tastings).

“There are too many tasting options for the number of visitors,” says DeLong. “If you’re a visitor, there’s an economic consideration and limited time.” 

Then, there’s the lack of spontaneity. “If you’re driving down one of the corridors and something catches your eye, the opportunity to pull over is great,” says Wendorf. “That’s half the fun of exploring.”

While he finds that people who make reservations tend to be more engaged with the brand—it’s that specific winery they wanted to spend their day and money—there are benefits to both camps. “On the other hand, the walk-in consumer is fun because you don’t know who they are,” Wendorf explains. It could be a buyer with interest, a big spender with time, or someone who could be a future fan. 

“You get to create a new brand ambassador—somebody who falls in love with what they experience,” he says. “The walk-in gives you a bigger opportunity for club conversions because they have no expectations. You can wow them. It’s a clean slate moment. Or, you can turn them off. If they walk in and you turn them away, even if the winery is empty, it’s a relationship lost.”

In Defense of Reservations

This isn’t to say a tasting room reservations system is a full-stop bad idea.

Sarah Citron, CEO of Bricoleur Vineyards, operates on a 90% reservation-based model. It allows the staff to curate every experience and ensures the kitchen is stocked and the hospitality team knows who’s coming. 

“Walk-ins add a beautiful spontaneity, but without the reservation infrastructure, it would be difficult to deliver the level of hospitality we’re committed to,” says Citron. “Reservations make the elevated experience financially and operationally sustainable, and attract that audience because it signals that what we offer is worth planning for.” 

Ehlers Estate is reservation-only, based on its permit, but that hasn’t proved to be an issue, according to director of sales and marketing Sandra DeMaria.  She finds that her guests are planners: 45% of people make reservations at least two weeks in advance. First time buyers, on average, make reservations at least three to five weeks in advance. Forty percent of guests are club members.

“They’re really planning way ahead before they come to the valley,” DeMaria says. “It has given us the opportunity to create experiences and have a connection before people come.” This approach has proved successful for Ehlers: On average, guests spend between $125 and $175 per visit, and usually purchase at least three bottles. 

For some consumers, planning detailed itineraries far in advance helps make the most of their travel investment. Visitors from Los Angeles spend, on average, nearly $4,000 per trip, according to Visit Napa Valley. If people are going to spend the money to come to Napa, stay overnight, and book the nanny, they want confirmed fun. 

Not all reservations are the same, staid, flight-and-lecture experience, either. Shadybrook Estate Winery tours guests around on horseback. Tank Garage hosts themed tasting events, including Italian Disco deejay sets and arcade parties. Ehlers Estate offers a Traitors-esque game played at communal tables where guests can interact.

What works for each winery depends on what their consumer wants. 

DeLong encourages her team to pivot if certain experiences aren’t selling or guests don’t seem engaged. “There will always be demand for incredible, bespoke, luxury-oriented, cerebral, high-touch experiences,” she says. “Those will always be popular with certain visitors. But the wineries who are able to be flexible, nimble, and curious while staying loyal to their brand ethos are the ones that are winning.”

Valley Rules

Due to rules and regulations of local ordinances, not every winery can welcome walk-ins. Daily and annual visitation limits are also dictated by county permits.

“The primary reason we are by reservation-only is due to our permit restrictions,” says Florencia Palmaz, CEO of Palmaz Vineyards. “We were never allowed to explore a different option of tour and tasting formats.” 

But it’s not a burden, Palmaz says. She finds that her team can forge closer relationships with their customers as a result. 

“Offering private tours allows each visitor to really explore the areas of wine that interest them,” she notes. “If a guest is interested in technology, then we will tailor the visit to their interest. If a guest is coming back for a second time, we are happy to pivot to a different area of winemaking or winegrowing.”

Citron agrees. “Today’s wine tourist wants meaning, not just wine. They’re looking for connection to the land, to the people making the wine, and to each other.”
